Stage 3 · Grammar

Imagining something that is not the case

Past forms, present meaning. That is the whole trick.

Read these three sentences.
  • If I were braver, I might be a firefighter.
  • We could volunteer more if we had more time.
  • I wouldn’t do a job if it were risky.
All three use past forms. Are they about the past?
Moving the verb one step back in time moves the situation one step away from reality.

The second conditional looks past-tense but is not about the past at all. If I had a car, I’d drive you is about now. The past form is doing something quite different from reporting past time: it is signalling distance from reality. Grammarians call this the unreal past, and once you see it as a distance marker rather than a time marker, the whole structure becomes coherent.

The contrast with the first conditional is a contrast in the speaker’s judgement, not in the facts of the world. If I get the job, I’ll move says you think it may well happen. If I got the job, I’d move says you doubt it, or that you are simply imagining. Both sentences are correct English about the same job; they tell your listener different things about your expectations.

That is why the second conditional is the natural language of daydreaming, of hypothetical questions, and of situations that are contrary to present fact. If I were stronger, I would stop that bully makes clear that you are not. If we won the lottery, we would give some to charity makes clear that you do not expect to. And the fixed advice formula If I were you, I’d… works precisely because both speakers know you are not them.

The same distance also produces politeness. It would be easier if you sent the file today is softer than It will be easier if you send the file today, because the unreal form presents the request as hypothetical rather than as an expectation. This use is very common in professional English.

was or were?If I were braver… is the careful form. If I was is common in speech.
AdviceIf I were you, I’d say something.

The past form is a distance marker, not a time marker. If I had time does not mean I had time yesterday. It means I do not have time now, and I am imagining that I did.

Never put would in the if half. Not If I would have more time but If I had more time. The would lives only in the result.

Might and could soften the result. I’d be a firefighter is confident; I might be a firefighter admits you are not sure. Both are correct.

The fixed phrase to learn. If I were you… is the standard way of giving advice in English. Not If I am you, and not In your place I will.

Full grammar reference — the unreal (second) conditional

What it is

The second conditional talks about a situation that is imaginary, unlikely or contrary to the present facts. Its shape is if + past simple, then would + base verb. The past form here does not refer to past time: it is a grammatical signal of distance from reality, which is why grammarians call it the unreal past.

What it means, and what it does

Moving the verb one step back in time moves the situation one step away from reality. If I am braver, I will be a firefighter would claim that this is a real prospect; If I were braver, I would be a firefighter says clearly that I am not brave enough and probably never will be. The listener reads the tense as a comment on how likely the speaker thinks it is.

When and why we use it

The second conditional looks past-tense but is not about the past at all. If I had a car, I’d drive you is about now. The past form is doing something quite different from reporting past time: it is signalling distance from reality. Grammarians call this the unreal past, and once you see it as a distance marker rather than a time marker, the whole structure becomes coherent.

The contrast with the first conditional is a contrast in the speaker’s judgement, not in the facts of the world. If I get the job, I’ll move says you think it may well happen. If I got the job, I’d move says you doubt it, or that you are simply imagining. Both sentences are correct English about the same job; they tell your listener different things about your expectations.

That is why the second conditional is the natural language of daydreaming, of hypothetical questions, and of situations that are contrary to present fact. If I were stronger, I would stop that bully makes clear that you are not. If we won the lottery, we would give some to charity makes clear that you do not expect to. And the fixed advice formula If I were you, I’d… works precisely because both speakers know you are not them.

The same distance also produces politeness. It would be easier if you sent the file today is softer than It will be easier if you send the file today, because the unreal form presents the request as hypothetical rather than as an expectation. This use is very common in professional English.

Typical situations

You need this for imagining different lives, answering hypothetical questions in interviews and discussions, giving advice, making a polite request, and explaining why you would or would not do something.

  • Imagining something untrue now — the present facts are the opposite.If I were stronger, I would stop that bully.
  • An unlikely future possibility — possible in theory, but the speaker doubts it.If we won the lottery, we would give some money to charity.
  • Giving advice — the fixed formula for a recommendation.If I were you, I’d take the first-aid course.
  • Asking a hypothetical question — a standard interview and discussion move.What would you do if you saw someone being robbed?
  • Talking about preferences and dreams — imagining a different life.If I could pick anywhere to live, I’d choose Iceland.
  • Being polite or tentative — the distance softens a request or an opinion.It would be easier if you sent the file today.
  • Refusing on principle — stating what you would not do.I wouldn’t do a job if it were risky or dangerous.

How it differs from similar structures

If I have time, I’ll help. (I probably will have time) · If I had time, I’d help. (I don’t have time). Same words, opposite messages.
If I were you… = advice · You should… = advice, more direct · You’d better… = advice with a warning attached. The conditional is the softest of the three.

How to build it

Standard: If + subject + past simple, + subject + would + base verb
Reversed: subject + would + base verb + if + subject + past simple  (no comma)
With be: If + subject + were …  (were for every person in careful English)
Other results: could / might + base verb
AffirmativeIf I had more time, I would volunteer.
Negative conditionIf she didn’t work nights, she would see the children more.
Negative resultIf I knew first aid, I wouldn’t panic.
QuestionWhat would you do if the plane caught fire?
Be in the conditionIf I were braver… · If he were here… — was is common in speech but were is standard.
With couldIf we had more time, we could volunteer more.
With mightIf people were better trained, they might act sooner.
Advice formulaIf I were you, I’d … — fixed; do not change the pronouns.

Saying it — contractions and stress

  • would reduces to ’d after a pronoun: I’d, he’d, they’d. Learners routinely fail to hear it and then produce the condition without a result modal.
  • ’d here is would; the base verb that follows proves it: I’d go (would) versus I’d gone (had).
  • would have in speech becomes would’ve /ˈwʊdəv/, which is often misheard and miswritten as would of.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • Were for all persons is the traditional form in the second conditional (If I were you, If he were here). Was is very common in informal speech, but If I were you is fixed and never varies.
  • No would in the if clause. If I would have more time is wrong in standard English — and it is the error learners from many language backgrounds make most persistently.
  • The past form carries no past meaning here. If I had a car is about now, not about yesterday.
  • Could in the if clause is possible because it is the past of can: If you could pick anywhere…
  • The choice between first and second conditional is the speaker’s judgement, not a fact about the world. If I get the job… and If I got the job… are both correct; they say different things about how likely you think it is.
  • For an imagined past situation, the verbs move back one step further: If I had known, I would have called. That is the third conditional, in Lesson 31.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • If I would have more time, I would volunteer. → If I had more time, I would volunteer.No would in the if clause.
  • If I was you, I’d take the course. → If I were you, I’d take the course.If I were you is a fixed expression.
  • If we won the lottery, we will give money to charity. → If we won the lottery, we would give money to charity.An unreal condition needs would, not will.
  • What you would do if you saw a crash? → What would you do if you saw a crash?The auxiliary comes before the subject in a question.
  • If she didn’t worked nights, she’d see them more. → If she didn’t work nights, she’d see them more.After didn’t, the base form.
  • If I would be braver, I’d be a firefighter. → If I were braver, I’d be a firefighter.The condition takes the past form of be.

More examples in context

  • untrue nowIf I were stronger, I would stop that bully.
  • unlikely futureIf we won the lottery, we’d give some of it to charity.
  • adviceIf I were you, I’d do the first-aid course before the trip.
  • hypothetical questionWhat would you do if you saw someone being robbed?
  • dreamIf I could pick anywhere in the world to live, I’d choose Reykjavík.
  • principleI wouldn’t take a job if it were genuinely dangerous.
  • with mightIf people knew first aid, more of them might help.
  • with couldWe could volunteer more if we had more free time.
  • softeningIt would help a lot if you let me know by Friday.
  • contrast with the real conditionalIf I get the promotion, I’ll move. If I got the promotion, I’d move — but I won’t.

A tip for remembering it

Remember the shape as ‘one step back’: the condition steps back into the past simple, and the result steps back from will to would. Both clauses move together. Then check the same thing every time: is there a would after if? If so, delete it and put the verb in the past simple.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. The second conditional imagines something untrue or unlikely: if + past simple, + would + base verb.
  2. The past form signals distance from reality, not past time.
  3. Never put would in the if clause.
  4. Use were for all persons in careful English; If I were you is fixed.
  5. Could and might can replace would in the result clause.
  6. First conditional = you think it may happen; second = you think it probably won’t.

Researchers at Berkeley have spent five years asking one question: what if you saw somebody in real danger? Most people say they their own life. In practice one in five has already done something heroic. The study found a pattern: if somebody a disaster themselves, they are three times more likely to act. Education matters too: , the more likely you are to help. Gender changes the answers people give, but not what they do. Men report heroism more often; women describe themselves as about their own actions. The researchers now train people online. If you the course, you become measurably less selfish.
